In [[mathematics]], the '''Browder–Minty theorem''' (sometimes called the '''Minty–Browder theorem''') states that a [[bounded operator|bounded]], [[continuous function|continuous]], [[coercive function|coercive]] and [[monotone function]] ''T'' from a [[real number|real]], [[separable space|separable]] [[reflexive space|reflexive]] [[Banach space]] ''X'' into its [[continuous dual space]] ''X''<sup>∗</sup> is automatically [[surjective]]. That is, for each [[continuous linear functional]] ''g''&nbsp;∈&nbsp;''X''<sup>∗</sup>, there exists a solution ''u''&nbsp;∈&nbsp;''X'' of the equation ''T''(''u'')&nbsp;=&nbsp;''g''. (Note that ''T'' itself is not required to be a [[linear map]].)

The theorem is named in honor of [[Felix Browder]] and [[George J. Minty]], who independently proved it.<ref name="Browder1967">{{cite journal|last1=Browder|first1=Felix E.|title=Existence and perturbation theorems for nonlinear maximal monotone operators in Banach spaces|journal=Bulletin of the American Mathematical Society|volume=73|issue=3|year=1967|pages=322–328|issn=0002-9904|doi=10.1090/S0002-9904-1967-11734-8|doi-access=free}}</ref>

==See also==

* [[Pseudo-monotone operator]]; pseudo-monotone operators obey a near-exact analogue of the Browder–Minty theorem.
